reason: The text contains multiple named characters who are regular people. Jacob (יַעֲקֹב) is depicted as an elderly father concerned about his family's survival during famine. His sons—Joseph (יוֹסֵף), Benjamin (בִּנְיָמִן), Simeon (שִׁמְעוֹן), Reuben (רְאוּבֵן), Judah (יְהוּדָה), and the other brothers—are portrayed as ordinary people engaged in commerce and familial relationships. Although Joseph has achieved a high administrative position in Egypt (מֹשֵׁ֖ל בְּכָל־ אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֔יִם), he remains a regular human being. The narrative consistently emphasizes their human emotions, concerns, and vulnerabilities, such as their fear of the Egyptian official and their grief over family separation.
